summary: Discusses algorithmic translation between IPv6 and IPv4 addresses using only static configuration. It defines a well-known prefix for such translation and allows networks to use their own prefixes instead.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6052 defines how a translator can encode an IPv4 address inside an IPv6 address and recover it later. It provides a shared prefix for general use and allows organizations to configure their own prefixes.

questions: what is the ipv6 well-known prefix 64:ff9b::/96
how is an ipv4 address embedded in ipv6
what is an ipv4-embedded ipv6 address
when should i use a network-specific prefix
subtitle: A fixed way to place an IPv4 address inside an IPv6 address for translation.

tldr.problem: IPv4/IPv6 translators and gateways need a predictable way to derive an address in one protocol from an address in the other using static configuration.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an IPv4-embedded IPv6 format containing a prefix, a 32-bit IPv4 address and, for some prefix lengths, a suffix. The prefix is either the Well-Known Prefix or an organization-specific prefix.
tldr.outcome: The RFC specifies the address format, translation algorithms, text notation and deployment guidance. It updates RFC 4291.

today: RFC 6052 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4291. It has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC in the unit metadata.

sections.title: Algorithmic Address Translation
sections.content:
This RFC is part of a series about IPv4/IPv6 translation. It specifies how to map an individual IPv6 address to an IPv4 address and back when the mapping is algorithmic, using statically configured information.

The rules can be used by packet translators and by other systems that manipulate addresses, including DNS proxies and application gateways. This document defines the address mapping itself; other specifications define the behavior of particular translators or gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: The same address-mapping recipe lets translators derive an IPv4 address from an IPv6 address and recover the IPv4 address in the reverse direction. Other documents define how particular translation devices operate.

sections.title: The IPv4-Embedded IPv6 Format
sections.content:
The Well-Known Prefix is 64:ff9b::/96. An IPv4-embedded IPv6 address consists of a prefix, the 32 bits of an IPv4 address and, for shorter prefixes, a suffix. Allowed prefix lengths are 32, 40, 48, 56, 64 and 96 bits. A Network-Specific Prefix must be unique to the organization using it.

Bits 64 through 71 form a reserved octet called u and must be zero. With prefix lengths below 96 bits, the IPv4 address is split around this octet. Remaining address bits are the suffix; they are reserved for future extensions and should be zero. A /96 prefix leaves no suffix.

The RFC calls addresses representing IPv4 nodes in an IPv6 network IPv4-converted addresses. IPv4-translatable addresses are assigned to IPv6 nodes for stateless translation. Both use the same format.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv6 address contains a prefix and the 32-bit IPv4 address. Some prefix lengths place a reserved zero octet between parts of the IPv4 address, and any remaining suffix bits should be zero.

sections.title: Building and Extracting the Address
sections.content:
To build an IPv4-embedded IPv6 address, concatenate the prefix, the 32 IPv4 address bits and any required suffix. If the prefix is shorter than 96 bits, insert the reserved zero octet at bits 64 through 71.

To extract an IPv4 address from a /96 prefix, take the final 32 bits. For other allowed prefix lengths, remove the reserved octet and extract the next 32 bits after the prefix. Text follows the IPv6 representation rules in RFC 4291. With the Well-Known Prefix or a /96 Network-Specific Prefix, the IPv4 address may be shown in dotted-decimal form at the end.
sections.plainLanguage: To encode, place the IPv4 bits after the prefix and insert the reserved zero octet when needed. To decode, remove that octet and copy out the 32 IPv4 bits.

sections.title: Choosing a Prefix for Translation
sections.content:
The Well-Known Prefix must not represent non-global IPv4 addresses. Translators must drop packets that combine it with a non-global address. It should not be used for IPv4-translatable addresses because derived more-specific prefixes are not supported for inter-domain advertisement; organizations should use a Network-Specific Prefix for that purpose.

For stateless translation, the RFC recommends a Network-Specific Prefix and recommends using the same prefix for IPv4-translatable and IPv4-converted addresses. That can let internal IPv6 traffic reach a translated-address host directly. Prefix length depends on the deployment scenario; the RFC gives /40 and /56 recommendations for some cases and /64 or /96 for others.

For stateful translation, the Well-Known Prefix is generally recommended, except in a scenario where it would represent non-global IPv4 addresses. If several stateful translators share a prefix, they must coordinate state or use different prefixes to avoid routing one connection to different translators.
sections.plainLanguage: Organizations choose a prefix based on how their translators work and which addresses they represent. The Well-Known Prefix cannot be used for private IPv4 addresses, and some deployments require an organization-specific prefix.

sections.title: Why the Prefix and Suffix Were Chosen
sections.content:
The RFC recommends a zero suffix. It considered reserving suffix bits for checksum neutrality or for a future port-range feature, but checksum neutrality can also be achieved by selecting a suitable Network-Specific Prefix. Reserved suffix bits remain available for a future extension.

The authors considered reusing the IPv4-mapped prefix, requesting a /32 or allocating a new /96. They chose a /96 Well-Known Prefix. The RFC explains that reusing the mapped prefix could cause existing systems to generate IPv4 rather than IPv6 packets. A /96 also permits the embedded IPv4 address to appear in dotted-decimal text form at the end.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC chose a /96 Well-Known Prefix and left suffix bits available for possible future use. This choice supports a readable address form and avoids reusing the existing IPv4-mapped prefix.

sections.title: Spoofing and Configuration Risks
sections.content:
A sender could use an IPv4-embedded IPv6 address as a source address so that, after translation, a packet appears to come from that IPv4 address. The RFC recommends reverse-path checks and verification that packets come from an authorized location.

Attackers could also try to make hosts, DNS gateways or translators use incorrect prefixes. Administrators must configure prefixes securely. Firewalls that filter IPv4 addresses should apply the same filtering to IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses representing those IPv4 addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: A false embedded address could make translated traffic appear to come from another IPv4 source. Networks should validate source paths, protect prefix configuration and apply firewall rules to both address forms.
